title: Beware big swings in midterm forecasts
contentHtml:
We’re approaching Labor Day — which has traditionally been considered the “real” starting point of midterm election campaigns. You’ll often hear a narrative that goes something like this: voters only get serious after Labor Day. They get back to their grind, their kids go back to school, and they finally start paying attention to politics (and football). So, you can’t really trust anything going on in the polls before then.

Selfishly, we’d love it if this campaign were only just getting started and there were wild gyrations in the polls and dramatic late swings in the race. Those tend to generate a lot of interest in the work we do here at Silver Bulletin.

But as responsible forecasters, we have to say: that’s usually not how congressional elections work, and that narrative is outdated in more than one way. For one thing, school starts in August in the large majority of the country. More importantly for our purposes, though, midterm races in the modern era tend not to change all that much between Labor Day and Election Day. The topline numbers in FLIPR, our midterm election model, have been quite steady since we launched it a few weeks ago, and we’d probably expect them to stay that way.

The national picture is more predictable than individual races

Let us clarify what we mean by this claim, because it would be easy to misconstrue this post.

We don’t mean that polls will be perfectly accurate. Obviously, you don’t need to go back very far to see examples of systematic, correlated polling errors — hello, 2016 and 2020 (and to a lesser extent 2024) — though note those were all presidential years rather than midterms. But how accurate the final polls are on Election Day is a different question from how much they drift or swing between September and November.

We also don’t mean there won’t be major shifts in individual races. Some states haven’t even held their primaries yet. And some important races have relatively little polling. But midterms are different in this respect than presidential years. A new poll in Michigan or Maine or South Carolina or Alaska pretty much affects that state and that state only.

Finally, it’s worth remembering that even small swings matter; our model is pretty sensitive at the margins. It’s probably going to be a blue year, but there are different shades of blue. But whether the 2026 national environment ends up looking closer to a pale eggshell or a dark navy will have massive implications for whether the Democratic Party’s year is spectacular or just okay. Democrats will need to win the popular vote by at least 3 points to be favored to win the House, and by at least 4 to 5 points if they want a double-digit majority. Even if they do win, this will affect how many House seats they pick up. (One can only assume that Hakeem Jeffries will want to avoid the problems his Republican counterparts are currently dealing with while trying to manage the slimmest House majority.)

This is even more the case in the Senate. Several traditionally Republican states — such as Texas and Ohio — lean slightly toward Democrats in large part because of favorable candidate quality matchups. But the national environment moving just a few points to the left would make Democrats clear favorites in those races. A shift of even a couple of points in the other direction would spell near-certain doom for Democrats’ chances of sweeping both chambers.

So yes, we hope you’ll keep checking in on FLIPR’s forecast. However, we’d probably bet against learning all that much more about the national environment until votes actually start getting counted on Nov. 3.
